notes.text: A widow — She that had a king, or rather a God, that was an husband to her, now was forsaken of God, and her king taken from her.

Because — Because of the servitude and oppression exercised among them: oppression by their rulers, and servitude more generally; keeping their servants beyond the year of jubilee, when they ought to be set at liberty. The straits - Those that pursued them overtook them in places where they could not escape.
She — Persons of all ages and ranks are in bitterness.
Wormwood — Wormwood and gall, are often made use of to signify great affliction.
This — Which follows, concerning the nature of God, and his good providences.
Faithfulness — In fulfilling thy promises to thy people.
Having declared his love to Timothy, 3-5 he exhorts him, " Be not ashamed of me." 6-14 And subjoins various examples, 15-18

He adds the twofold proposition,

1. "Be strong,"

2. "Commit the ministry" to faithful men,. ii. 1, 2 The former is treated of, 3-13 The latter, 14 With farther directions concerning his own behaviour, 15- iv.8

3. "Come quickly." Here St. Paul, 9

1. Mentions his being left alone, 10-12

2. Directs to bring his books, 13

3. Gives a caution concerning Alexander, 14, 15

4. Observes the inconstancy of men, and the faithfulness of God, 16-18

4. "Come before winter." Salutations, 19-21 III. The concluding blessing, 22 2nd TIMOTHY

Whom I serve from my forefathers — That is, whom both I and my ancestors served, with a pure conscience - He always worshipped God according to his conscience, both before and after his conversion One who stands on the verge of life is much refreshed by the remembrance of his predecessors, to whom he is going.
Being mindful of thy tears — Perhaps frequently shed, as well as at the apostle's last parting with him.
Which dwelt — A word not applied to a transient guest, but only to a settled inhabitant. First - Probably this was before Timothy was born, yet not beyond St. Paul's memory.
Wherefore — Because I remember this. I remind thee of stirring up - Literally, blowing up the coals into a flame. The gift of God - All the spiritual gifts, which the grace of God has given thee.

And let nothing discourage thee, for God hath not given us — That is, the spirit which God hath given us Christians, is not the spirit of fear - Or cowardice. But of power - Banishing fear. And love and sobriety - These animate us in our duties to God, our brethren, and ourselves. Power and sobriety are two good extremes. Love is between, the tie and temperament of both; preventing the two bad extremes of fearfulness and rashness. More is said concerning power, ver. 8; concerning love, chap. ii, 14, &c.; concerning sobriety, chap. iii, 1, &c.

Therefore be not thou ashamed — When fear is banished, evil shame also flees away. Of the testimony of our Lord - The gospel, and of testifying the truth of it to all men. Nor of me - The cause of the servants of God doing his work, cannot be separated from the cause of God himself. But be thou partaker of the afflictions - Which I endure for the gospel's sake. According to the power of God - This which overcomes all things is nervously described in the two next verses.

Who hath saved us — By faith. The love of the Father, the grace of our saviour, and the whole economy of salvation, are here admirably described. Having called us with an holy calling - Which is all from God, and claims us all for God. According to his own purpose and grace - That is, his own gracious purpose. Which was given us - Fixed for our advantage, before the world began.

By the appearing of our saviour — This implies his whole abode upon earth. Who hath abolished death - Taken away its sting, and turned it into a blessing. And hath brought life and immortality to light - Hath clearly revealed by the gospel that immortal life which he hath purchased for us.
That which I have committed to him — My soul. Until that day - Of his final appearing.
The pattern of sound words — The model of pure, wholesome doctrine.
The good thing — This wholesome doctrine.

glossa.text: *Paul an apostle.* First the Apostle salutes, then he gives thanks for the good which he has, where he shows his own desire of seeing him. Afterwards he admonishes him to preaching, and to the patience of martyrdom, by his own example and in other ways. Thence he says what sort of men they shall be in the last days: at last, concerning the time of his own release, which is at hand. *By the will of God.* Not by my merits, as if he should say: In like manner thou also hast been sent freely, and therefore art the more bound to the grace that is to be preached.

*I give thanks.* He gives thanks for his [Timothy's] good, commending the grace of faith which is in Christ.

*Remembrance.* For Timothy wept when he was dismissed by Paul, being ready to go with him unto all perils. What therefore he had while present, let him hold while absent, *receiving also the recollection of the faith* which may admonish thee, since it was firm even in women.

*For which cause.* His faith having been commended, he exhorts him to preach it without fear and without shame. *By the imposition of hands.* That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which thou hast received for the establishing of the Church, for the accomplishing of miracles, for every observance of religion.

*Of fear.* Peter, being troubled by fear, denied Christ. Whence: *Fear ye not them that kill the body ((Matth. XXVI.))* Of this fear we have not received the spirit, but of that fear of which the Lord says: *Fear him who is able to destroy both body and soul into hell.* For the Holy Spirit gives a fear not of the world, but of God, who is able to destroy into the hell of fire.

*Be not thou therefore.* He teaches that constancy is to be had, and that there is no shame to be felt in the profession: for it is not such that one should be ashamed in it: because as Christ was seen a man, yet by his deeds he appeared God; although he was crucified, yet he rose again from the dead, and, while many beheld it and a cloud received him, ascended into heaven. Where therefore weakness is supposed, there power appears.
*Who hath delivered us.* It is fitting to render a return to him who delivers: And since we are not able worthily to answer his benefits, let us at least perform his embassy faithfully and urgently.

*Who hath destroyed.* Death, as being conquered, is not to be feared for the faith of Christ. *But hath illuminated.* Whither these things look, he there opens: *Having a form. Through the Gospel.* God showed forth incorruptible life, which before was unknown; he showed it, I say, through the preaching of the Gospel, whose preacher is Paul.

*Wherein I am appointed.* Here he exhorts by his own example. *A preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher,* etc. But what is the reason, since he continually calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles? he wishes, forsooth, to persuade that the Gentiles also have been called into the inheritance of God, and therefore are not to be driven back from the fellowship of the faith.

*For I know.* As if he should say: Therefore *I am not confounded,* that is, I fail, or I do not suffer in vain, because he has promised and is truthful and powerful: and therefore I have believed that very one who will render to me. *Because he is able.* He is secure through the hope and the magnificence of the Saviour, because what he commends to him is in safety. And to him he commends his own salvation, that here suffering for him he may find salvation with him when he shall have begun to judge, so that, punishing the unfaithful, he may pronounce this man worthy of eternal life.

*Having a form.* Here he shows whither the things foretold about himself look. As if he should say: Thus I labour in this office committed to me: in like manner therefore thou also, having a form, etc.

*Of whom is Phigellus and Hermogenes.* These were with the Apostle feignedly, that they might find matter of calumny: but after they saw themselves made manifest, they withdrew from him.

notes.text: Lord, increase our faith — That we may thus forgive, and may neither offend nor be offended. Matt. xvii, 20.

And he said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed — If ye had the least measure of true faith, no instance of duty would be too hard for you. Ye would say to this sycamine tree - This seems to have been a kind of proverbial expression.
But which of you — But is it not meet that you should first obey, and then triumph? Though still with a deep sense of your utter unprofitableness.
Doth he thank that servant — Does he account himself obliged to him?

When ye have done all, say, We are unprofitable servants — For a man cannot profit God. Happy is he who Judges himself an unprofitable servant: miserable is he whom God pronounces such. But though we are unprofitable to him, our serving him is not unprofitable to us. For he is pleased to give by his grace a value to our good works, which in consequence of his promise entitles us to an eternal reward.

glossa.text: *Increase.* Since he had said above ((Luc. XVI)): *He that is faithful in that which is least,* etc. The apostles, who in that which was another's and in that which was least, that is, in the contempt of earthly things, had been faithful, ask that faith be increased in what is their own and greater, that they who from faith already have the beginnings of virtue may advance in the same, until they come to perfection.

*To the mulberry tree.* By the mulberry, of blood-red colour, whose fruit and twigs are ruddy, the Gospel of the cross is expressed, which by the faith of the apostles was uprooted out of the nation of the Jews (in which, as in the stock of the race, the word of preaching was held) and transplanted into the sea of the Gentiles; to which the parable subjoined concerning the ministers of the word also fits. The leaves of the mulberry laid under a serpent bring death, and the word of the cross, as it confers all wholesome things, takes away all noxious ones. The fruit of the mulberry is white in flower, when formed grows red, in ripeness turns black: so the devil, of one shining red with the flower of the angelic nature and with power, by prevaricating bristled up, a terror, in odour, who is shut out through faith.

*But which of you,* etc. The servant ploughing or feeding is the doctor of the Church, of whom it is said: *No man putting his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom ((Luc. IX))* of God. And the Lord says to Peter: *Feed my sheep ((Joan. XXI))*. Which servant returns from the field when, the work of preaching being intermitted, returning as it were to the court of conscience he goes over his own words or deeds; whom the Lord does not at once bid to pass out of this life and be cherished in eternal rest, but to prepare at home what he may sup on, that is, after the labour of open speech, to display the humility of his own manner of life, for in such a conscience God sups.
*And minister to me.* He ministers to his Maker who, considering his nature and greatly fearing his judgments, humbles himself from his own virtues. For a minister is so called from a lesser estate.

*So you also.* After he has exhorted to the perfection of faith, through which wonderful works are done even against the nature of things, he warns that no one should glory of his own works, but that by how much faith is outwardly more excellent in virtues, by so much the conscience within should be more humble, because we owe obedience to the Lord by right. *Unprofitable servants.* If a man exacts from a man who is his servant not a uniform but a manifold ministry, and gives him no thanks, how much more ought you who without me can do nothing not to practise the use of one work or one labour only, but always to increase former things with new zeal, nor should you boast, because you serve well.

*What we ought to do.* He who came to minister and not to be ministered unto has made us debtors to himself, that not trusting in our own works, but fearing his examination, when all things are fulfilled which have been commanded, we may recognize that we are unperfected, so long as we are pilgrims from God.

Like a tree that's planted by the water
Like an ant on a stick both ends of which are burning
O Holy Spirit, Root of life

praise.title: Holy Spirit You Are Welcome Here
Pass Me Not, O Gentle Savior

echoes.text: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The greeting 'Grace, mercy, and peace' echoes the Aaronic priestly blessing, where the LORD is asked to 'be gracious' and to 'give peace.' The triad of grace and peace in Paul's salutations draws on this benedictory form.

echoes.text: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.
echoes.note: Paul styles his apostleship as serving 'the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus.' The Deuteronomic covenant blessing frames clinging to the LORD as the source of 'life and length of days,' an OT matrix for the promise-of-life language Paul Christologizes here.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: The 'promise' according to which Paul is sent recalls the patriarchal covenant promise to Abraham and his seed; Pauline 'promise' theology consistently roots in this Genesis covenant. Faint here, marked contested.

echoes.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The 'pure conscience' with which Paul serves echoes the OT ideal of the 'pure heart and clean hands' required to stand before God. The psalm's purity-of-heart standard underlies the conscience language transposed into Pauline interiority.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might. These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
echoes.note: The 'sincere faith' that lived first in grandmother Lois and mother Eunice and now in Timothy enacts the Shema's command to bind covenant faith on the heart and teach it diligently to children across generations. The intergenerational transmission of faith is the Deuteronomic catechetical ideal.

echoes.text: For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children; that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children, that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments,
echoes.note: The chain of faith from grandmother to mother to son mirrors the psalm's mandate that fathers teach the next generation so that children yet unborn would set their hope in God. Timothy's inherited 'sincere faith' embodies this generational handing-down.

echoes.text: And the vision of that dream was this: He saw Onias, him that was high priest, a noble and good man, reverend in bearing, yet gentle in manner and well-spoken, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue, with outstretched hands invoking blessings on the whole body of the Jews:
echoes.note: Serving God 'as my forefathers did' with a 'pure conscience' presents Paul's gospel as continuous with ancestral Jewish piety; 2 Maccabees praises the high priest Onias as a man of upright conscience and ancestral devotion. Deuterocanonical conscience language is faint background.

echoes.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
echoes.note: The plea for a 'clean heart' and right spirit parallels Paul's claim to serve God with a pure conscience; the conscience motif develops the OT clean-heart ideal. Faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: Paul's 'unceasing memory' and remembering 'night and day' draws on the OT idiom of a fragrant memorial / remembrance before God; Genesis introduces the 'pleasing aroma' the LORD remembers. The remembrance language is faint.

echoes.text: My son, listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching:
echoes.note: The faith received specifically through grandmother and mother recalls the wisdom tradition's appeal to heed 'your mother's teaching.' The maternal pedagogy motif faintly underlies the naming of Lois and Eunice.

echoes.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
echoes.note: 'God didn't give us a spirit of fear' answers the LORD's charge to Joshua, 'be strong and courageous; do not be afraid,' precisely as Timothy steps into a Joshua-like succession of leadership. The not-fearing-but-strong commission undergirds the whole exhortation.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Stirring up 'the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands' recalls Moses commissioning Joshua by the laying on of hands so that he was filled with the spirit of wisdom. The ordination-by-imposition-of-hands motif is rooted in this Mosaic succession.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.
echoes.note: Joshua was 'full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him,' the precise pattern Paul invokes: a spiritual gift conferred through imposition of hands by the predecessor. Strongly parallels Timothy's reception of the charisma.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Spirit God gives, 'of power, love, and self-control' rather than fear, recalls the messianic endowment of the Spirit of wisdom, counsel, and might resting on the shoot of Jesse. The enumerated Spirit-qualities echo Isaiah's catalog of the Spirit's gifts.

echoes.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Don't be afraid, for I am with you... I will strengthen you' parallels Paul's denial that God gives a spirit of fear and his assertion of a spirit of power. Isaiah's salvation-oracle formula of fearlessness-through-divine-strength stands behind the verse.

echoes.text: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The 'spirit of power' contrasted with fear echoes 'not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit'; the divine Spirit as the true source of effective strength. Faint conceptual link, marked contested.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'Don't be ashamed of the testimony' draws on the Servant's resolve: 'I have set my face like a flint, and I know I will not be put to shame.' The vindication-of-the-unashamed-witness motif shapes Paul's appeal to Timothy to embrace suffering without shame.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of your testimonies before kings, and will not be put to shame' directly anticipates Paul's call not to be ashamed of the testimony and of his chains. The unashamed public confession before rulers is the psalmist's posture.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: God 'saved us and called us... not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace' restates the Deuteronomic logic of election: the LORD set his love on Israel not because of their numbers or merit but because he loved them and kept his oath. Election by sheer gracious purpose is the OT root.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: Christ 'who abolished death' echoes the eschatological promise that the LORD 'will swallow up death forever.' The abolition-of-death motif is the climactic Isaianic hope now realized in the Savior's appearing.

echoes.text: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being;
echoes.note: Christ 'brought life and immortality to light' resonates with Wisdom's claim that God created humanity for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity. The deuterocanonical immortality/incorruption vocabulary directly underlies Paul's athanasia language.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality;
echoes.note: The hope that 'the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God' and their 'hope is full of immortality' parallels the life-and-immortality brought to light through the gospel. Wisdom's immortality theology is the closest Second-Temple antecedent.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: 'He who believes will not be put to shame' is a recurrent Pauline shame-text; here it faintly informs the unashamed-testimony theme even without citation. Marked contested.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: 'I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death' provides an OT oracle of death's defeat behind Christ's abolishing of death. Faint, overlapping with Isaiah 25:8.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The disclosure of 'life and immortality' resonates with Daniel's resurrection hope of awaking to everlasting life. The apocalyptic immortality promise is a faint backdrop to the gospel's bringing of imperishable life to light.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: Paul's appointment as 'a teacher of the Gentiles' enacts the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations,' that salvation might reach the ends of the earth. His Gentile herald-role fulfills Isaiah's light-to-the-nations mandate.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'Yet I am not ashamed' in the midst of suffering reprises the Servant's flint-faced confidence that he will not be put to shame. The Servant's unashamed endurance models Paul's own.

echoes.text: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.
echoes.note: 'I know whom I have believed, and... he is able to guard that which I have committed to him' echoes 'Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me.' The committing/entrusting of oneself to the faithful God parallels the psalmist's deposit. Marked contested.

echoes.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you. In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
echoes.note: 'In God I trust; I will not be afraid' parallels Paul's confident 'I know whom I have believed' and lack of shame. Faint trust-formula resonance.

echoes.text: Therefore you shall lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul. You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them your children, talking of them, when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
echoes.note: 'Guard' the good deposit through the Spirit echoes the command to lay up God's words in heart and soul, binding and teaching them. The entrusted-treasure-of-the-word imagery is rooted in Deuteronomy's commands to keep and transmit the torah.

echoes.text: Take firm hold of instruction. Don’t let her go. Keep her, for she is your life.
echoes.note: 'Take hold of instruction; do not let go; keep her, for she is your life' closely parallels 'hold the pattern of sound words' and 'guard' the deposit. The wisdom command to grip and guard saving instruction undergirds Paul's exhortation.

echoes.text: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.
echoes.note: Holding 'the pattern of sound words' and guarding 'that good thing committed to you' draws on the Deuteronomic charge to add nothing and take nothing from the commanded word but to keep it. The deposit-of-teaching motif reflects covenant-word preservation.

echoes.text: My son, if you will receive my words, and store up my commandments within you;
echoes.note: Receiving words and 'treasuring up' commandments parallels the entrusted good deposit to be guarded. Faint wisdom-deposit link, marked contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: Zechariah's word that the great 'mountain' shall become a plain before Zerubbabel by the Spirit, not by might, is the canonical pairing of faith with the moving/leveling of an immovable obstacle. The mountain-removed-by-faith logic gives Coherence with 'faith like a mustard seed,' though Luke uses a sycamore-into-sea rather than a mountain, lowering Volume.

echoes.text: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;
echoes.note: The psalm's confidence even 'though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of an immovable thing thrown into the sea, here recast as the work of faith. The verbal overlap (uprooted/carried into the sea) is real but the figure is proverbial, so it is faint.

echoes.text: He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains were crumbled. The age-old hills collapsed. His ways are eternal.
echoes.note: The theophany that scatters the everlasting mountains coheres with the faith-moves-mountains topos behind the uprooted-tree saying. The connection is conceptual and diffuse, so confidence is low.

echoes.text: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you, neither shall my covenant of peace be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'the mountains may depart' as a figure of cosmic upheaval feeds the same stock of immovable-object-displaced imagery that the mustard-seed/sycamore saying exploits. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him, that you make your ways perfect?
echoes.note: Eliphaz asks whether a man can be profitable to God or whether it is gain to the Almighty that one is righteous, the wisdom premise that human service places God under no obligation. This grounds the 'we are unworthy servants, we have only done our duty' logic; moderate Coherence with the servant parable.

echoes.text: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?
echoes.note: Elihu's 'if you are righteous, what do you give him?' states the same theology of non-meritorious obedience underlying the unprofitable-servant saying. Recurrence of the motif across Job strengthens the Availability and Coherence, though there is no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.
echoes.note: The image of servants' eyes fixed on the hand of their master, waiting on his command, supplies the master-servant deference picture the parable assumes. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: God's claim that the Israelites are his servants whom he brought out of Egypt frames Israel's whole obedience as owed service, the covenantal backdrop to 'we have only done what was our duty.' Faint, diffuse, contested.

notes.text: The burden — The prophet seems to speak of these grievous things, as a burden which he himself groaned under.

Therefore — Because the wicked go on with impunity. The law - The whole law, moral, ceremonial, and judicial. Is slacked - Is slighted, and not observed. Go forth - From magistrates, Judges, and public officers. Doth compass about - As it were besieges, with design to oppress and ruin.

Upon my watch — I will stand as a watchman on my watch- tower. He - The Lord. Reproved - Called to give an account of the mysteriousness of providence; either to satisfy doubters, or to silence quarrellers.

Upon tables — What was of publick concern, and therefore to be published, was anciently written or engraven upon tables, smooth stones, or wood, and then hung up in a publick place to be read. May run - That none may need to stop, but every one may plainly and clearly discern what is written.
At the end — When the period appointed of God shall come. Shall speak - Be accomplished, and not disappoint your expectation.

Which is lifted up — That proudly contests with the justice and wisdom of the Divine Providence, and provides for his own safety by his own wit. The just - The humble and upright one, who adores the depth of divine providence, and is persuaded of the truth of divine promises. Shall live - Supports himself, by a firm expectation of the deliverance of Zion.
Fret not — Because they prosper in their wicked enterprizes.
Commit — All thy cares and business, and necessities, commend to God by fervent prayer.
Judgment — It shall be as visible to men, as the light of the sun, at noon-day.
Rest — Do not repine at his dealings, but quietly submit to his will, and wait for his help.
Fret not — Either against the sinner for his success; or against God. Do evil - If grief arise in thee, take care that it do not transport thee to sin.
The earth — This for the most part was literally fulfilled in that state of the church.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* This psalm is as it were the garment of Christ, which covers his whole body with precepts, and protects it from adversities, and cherishes it as in the bosom of counsel. It is a draught against those who murmur at the flowering of the wicked and the toil of the good, as though all things were done by chance, so that, spurning God, they cleave to the world. The Church therefore admonishes that no one imitate the malignant, but that whatever good is hoped for be sought from the Lord, who gives things profitable and eternal.

*The herbs of the grasses.* ((AUG.)) It is now winter, etc., *as far as* because it hath not yet appeared what we shall be.

((AUG., CASS.)) Herbs not of gardens, but of grasses, that is, the meanest, which spring up of themselves through the fields. *Hay,* the noble, who prosper easily; herbs, the middling: but both those quickly wither and these fall away.

*Cease.* ((AUG.)) Anger is sudden, fury lasting; but both are to be forsaken, through which men sin. ((CASS.)) This is said to him who is still weak, etc., *as far as* by doing it he flourishes for a time.

notes.text: Having declared his love to Timothy, 3-5 he exhorts him, " Be not ashamed of me." 6-14 And subjoins various examples, 15-18

He adds the twofold proposition,

1. "Be strong,"

2. "Commit the ministry" to faithful men,. ii. 1, 2 The former is treated of, 3-13 The latter, 14 With farther directions concerning his own behaviour, 15- iv.8

3. "Come quickly." Here St. Paul, 9

1. Mentions his being left alone, 10-12

2. Directs to bring his books, 13

3. Gives a caution concerning Alexander, 14, 15

4. Observes the inconstancy of men, and the faithfulness of God, 16-18

4. "Come before winter." Salutations, 19-21 III. The concluding blessing, 22 2nd TIMOTHY

Whom I serve from my forefathers — That is, whom both I and my ancestors served, with a pure conscience - He always worshipped God according to his conscience, both before and after his conversion One who stands on the verge of life is much refreshed by the remembrance of his predecessors, to whom he is going.
Being mindful of thy tears — Perhaps frequently shed, as well as at the apostle's last parting with him.
Which dwelt — A word not applied to a transient guest, but only to a settled inhabitant. First - Probably this was before Timothy was born, yet not beyond St. Paul's memory.
Wherefore — Because I remember this. I remind thee of stirring up - Literally, blowing up the coals into a flame. The gift of God - All the spiritual gifts, which the grace of God has given thee.

And let nothing discourage thee, for God hath not given us — That is, the spirit which God hath given us Christians, is not the spirit of fear - Or cowardice. But of power - Banishing fear. And love and sobriety - These animate us in our duties to God, our brethren, and ourselves. Power and sobriety are two good extremes. Love is between, the tie and temperament of both; preventing the two bad extremes of fearfulness and rashness. More is said concerning power, ver. 8; concerning love, chap. ii, 14, &c.; concerning sobriety, chap. iii, 1, &c.

Therefore be not thou ashamed — When fear is banished, evil shame also flees away. Of the testimony of our Lord - The gospel, and of testifying the truth of it to all men. Nor of me - The cause of the servants of God doing his work, cannot be separated from the cause of God himself. But be thou partaker of the afflictions - Which I endure for the gospel's sake. According to the power of God - This which overcomes all things is nervously described in the two next verses.

Who hath saved us — By faith. The love of the Father, the grace of our saviour, and the whole economy of salvation, are here admirably described. Having called us with an holy calling - Which is all from God, and claims us all for God. According to his own purpose and grace - That is, his own gracious purpose. Which was given us - Fixed for our advantage, before the world began.

By the appearing of our saviour — This implies his whole abode upon earth. Who hath abolished death - Taken away its sting, and turned it into a blessing. And hath brought life and immortality to light - Hath clearly revealed by the gospel that immortal life which he hath purchased for us.
That which I have committed to him — My soul. Until that day - Of his final appearing.
The pattern of sound words — The model of pure, wholesome doctrine.
The good thing — This wholesome doctrine.

glossa.text: *Paul an apostle.* First the Apostle salutes, then he gives thanks for the good which he has, where he shows his own desire of seeing him. Afterwards he admonishes him to preaching, and to the patience of martyrdom, by his own example and in other ways. Thence he says what sort of men they shall be in the last days: at last, concerning the time of his own release, which is at hand. *By the will of God.* Not by my merits, as if he should say: In like manner thou also hast been sent freely, and therefore art the more bound to the grace that is to be preached.

*I give thanks.* He gives thanks for his [Timothy's] good, commending the grace of faith which is in Christ.

*Remembrance.* For Timothy wept when he was dismissed by Paul, being ready to go with him unto all perils. What therefore he had while present, let him hold while absent, *receiving also the recollection of the faith* which may admonish thee, since it was firm even in women.

*For which cause.* His faith having been commended, he exhorts him to preach it without fear and without shame. *By the imposition of hands.* That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which thou hast received for the establishing of the Church, for the accomplishing of miracles, for every observance of religion.

*Of fear.* Peter, being troubled by fear, denied Christ. Whence: *Fear ye not them that kill the body ((Matth. XXVI.))* Of this fear we have not received the spirit, but of that fear of which the Lord says: *Fear him who is able to destroy both body and soul into hell.* For the Holy Spirit gives a fear not of the world, but of God, who is able to destroy into the hell of fire.

*Be not thou therefore.* He teaches that constancy is to be had, and that there is no shame to be felt in the profession: for it is not such that one should be ashamed in it: because as Christ was seen a man, yet by his deeds he appeared God; although he was crucified, yet he rose again from the dead, and, while many beheld it and a cloud received him, ascended into heaven. Where therefore weakness is supposed, there power appears.
*Who hath delivered us.* It is fitting to render a return to him who delivers: And since we are not able worthily to answer his benefits, let us at least perform his embassy faithfully and urgently.

*Who hath destroyed.* Death, as being conquered, is not to be feared for the faith of Christ. *But hath illuminated.* Whither these things look, he there opens: *Having a form. Through the Gospel.* God showed forth incorruptible life, which before was unknown; he showed it, I say, through the preaching of the Gospel, whose preacher is Paul.

*Wherein I am appointed.* Here he exhorts by his own example. *A preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher,* etc. But what is the reason, since he continually calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles? he wishes, forsooth, to persuade that the Gentiles also have been called into the inheritance of God, and therefore are not to be driven back from the fellowship of the faith.

*For I know.* As if he should say: Therefore *I am not confounded,* that is, I fail, or I do not suffer in vain, because he has promised and is truthful and powerful: and therefore I have believed that very one who will render to me. *Because he is able.* He is secure through the hope and the magnificence of the Saviour, because what he commends to him is in safety. And to him he commends his own salvation, that here suffering for him he may find salvation with him when he shall have begun to judge, so that, punishing the unfaithful, he may pronounce this man worthy of eternal life.

*Having a form.* Here he shows whither the things foretold about himself look. As if he should say: Thus I labour in this office committed to me: in like manner therefore thou also, having a form, etc.

*Of whom is Phigellus and Hermogenes.* These were with the Apostle feignedly, that they might find matter of calumny: but after they saw themselves made manifest, they withdrew from him.

notes.text: Lord, increase our faith — That we may thus forgive, and may neither offend nor be offended. Matt. xvii, 20.

And he said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed — If ye had the least measure of true faith, no instance of duty would be too hard for you. Ye would say to this sycamine tree - This seems to have been a kind of proverbial expression.
But which of you — But is it not meet that you should first obey, and then triumph? Though still with a deep sense of your utter unprofitableness.
Doth he thank that servant — Does he account himself obliged to him?

When ye have done all, say, We are unprofitable servants — For a man cannot profit God. Happy is he who Judges himself an unprofitable servant: miserable is he whom God pronounces such. But though we are unprofitable to him, our serving him is not unprofitable to us. For he is pleased to give by his grace a value to our good works, which in consequence of his promise entitles us to an eternal reward.

glossa.text: *Increase.* Since he had said above ((Luc. XVI)): *He that is faithful in that which is least,* etc. The apostles, who in that which was another's and in that which was least, that is, in the contempt of earthly things, had been faithful, ask that faith be increased in what is their own and greater, that they who from faith already have the beginnings of virtue may advance in the same, until they come to perfection.

*To the mulberry tree.* By the mulberry, of blood-red colour, whose fruit and twigs are ruddy, the Gospel of the cross is expressed, which by the faith of the apostles was uprooted out of the nation of the Jews (in which, as in the stock of the race, the word of preaching was held) and transplanted into the sea of the Gentiles; to which the parable subjoined concerning the ministers of the word also fits. The leaves of the mulberry laid under a serpent bring death, and the word of the cross, as it confers all wholesome things, takes away all noxious ones. The fruit of the mulberry is white in flower, when formed grows red, in ripeness turns black: so the devil, of one shining red with the flower of the angelic nature and with power, by prevaricating bristled up, a terror, in odour, who is shut out through faith.

*But which of you,* etc. The servant ploughing or feeding is the doctor of the Church, of whom it is said: *No man putting his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom ((Luc. IX))* of God. And the Lord says to Peter: *Feed my sheep ((Joan. XXI))*. Which servant returns from the field when, the work of preaching being intermitted, returning as it were to the court of conscience he goes over his own words or deeds; whom the Lord does not at once bid to pass out of this life and be cherished in eternal rest, but to prepare at home what he may sup on, that is, after the labour of open speech, to display the humility of his own manner of life, for in such a conscience God sups.
*And minister to me.* He ministers to his Maker who, considering his nature and greatly fearing his judgments, humbles himself from his own virtues. For a minister is so called from a lesser estate.

*So you also.* After he has exhorted to the perfection of faith, through which wonderful works are done even against the nature of things, he warns that no one should glory of his own works, but that by how much faith is outwardly more excellent in virtues, by so much the conscience within should be more humble, because we owe obedience to the Lord by right. *Unprofitable servants.* If a man exacts from a man who is his servant not a uniform but a manifold ministry, and gives him no thanks, how much more ought you who without me can do nothing not to practise the use of one work or one labour only, but always to increase former things with new zeal, nor should you boast, because you serve well.

*What we ought to do.* He who came to minister and not to be ministered unto has made us debtors to himself, that not trusting in our own works, but fearing his examination, when all things are fulfilled which have been commanded, we may recognize that we are unperfected, so long as we are pilgrims from God.

hymns.title: O Holy Spirit, Root of life
Faith, while trees are still in blossom
God of love and God of power
Walk in the light of God's counsel
Like a tree that's planted by the water

praise.title: Holy Spirit You Are Welcome Here

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The greeting 'Grace, mercy, and peace' echoes the Aaronic priestly blessing, where the LORD is asked to 'be gracious' and to 'give peace.' The triad of grace and peace in Paul's salutations draws on this benedictory form.

echoes.text: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.
echoes.note: Paul styles his apostleship as serving 'the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus.' The Deuteronomic covenant blessing frames clinging to the LORD as the source of 'life and length of days,' an OT matrix for the promise-of-life language Paul Christologizes here.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: The 'promise' according to which Paul is sent recalls the patriarchal covenant promise to Abraham and his seed; Pauline 'promise' theology consistently roots in this Genesis covenant. Faint here, marked contested.

echoes.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The 'pure conscience' with which Paul serves echoes the OT ideal of the 'pure heart and clean hands' required to stand before God. The psalm's purity-of-heart standard underlies the conscience language transposed into Pauline interiority.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might. These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
echoes.note: The 'sincere faith' that lived first in grandmother Lois and mother Eunice and now in Timothy enacts the Shema's command to bind covenant faith on the heart and teach it diligently to children across generations. The intergenerational transmission of faith is the Deuteronomic catechetical ideal.

echoes.text: For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children; that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children, that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments,
echoes.note: The chain of faith from grandmother to mother to son mirrors the psalm's mandate that fathers teach the next generation so that children yet unborn would set their hope in God. Timothy's inherited 'sincere faith' embodies this generational handing-down.

echoes.text: And the vision of that dream was this: He saw Onias, him that was high priest, a noble and good man, reverend in bearing, yet gentle in manner and well-spoken, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue, with outstretched hands invoking blessings on the whole body of the Jews:
echoes.note: Serving God 'as my forefathers did' with a 'pure conscience' presents Paul's gospel as continuous with ancestral Jewish piety; 2 Maccabees praises the high priest Onias as a man of upright conscience and ancestral devotion. Deuterocanonical conscience language is faint background.

echoes.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
echoes.note: The plea for a 'clean heart' and right spirit parallels Paul's claim to serve God with a pure conscience; the conscience motif develops the OT clean-heart ideal. Faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: Paul's 'unceasing memory' and remembering 'night and day' draws on the OT idiom of a fragrant memorial / remembrance before God; Genesis introduces the 'pleasing aroma' the LORD remembers. The remembrance language is faint.

echoes.text: My son, listen to your father’s instruction, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching:
echoes.note: The faith received specifically through grandmother and mother recalls the wisdom tradition's appeal to heed 'your mother's teaching.' The maternal pedagogy motif faintly underlies the naming of Lois and Eunice.

echoes.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
echoes.note: 'God didn't give us a spirit of fear' answers the LORD's charge to Joshua, 'be strong and courageous; do not be afraid,' precisely as Timothy steps into a Joshua-like succession of leadership. The not-fearing-but-strong commission undergirds the whole exhortation.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Stirring up 'the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands' recalls Moses commissioning Joshua by the laying on of hands so that he was filled with the spirit of wisdom. The ordination-by-imposition-of-hands motif is rooted in this Mosaic succession.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.
echoes.note: Joshua was 'full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him,' the precise pattern Paul invokes: a spiritual gift conferred through imposition of hands by the predecessor. Strongly parallels Timothy's reception of the charisma.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Spirit God gives, 'of power, love, and self-control' rather than fear, recalls the messianic endowment of the Spirit of wisdom, counsel, and might resting on the shoot of Jesse. The enumerated Spirit-qualities echo Isaiah's catalog of the Spirit's gifts.

echoes.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Don't be afraid, for I am with you... I will strengthen you' parallels Paul's denial that God gives a spirit of fear and his assertion of a spirit of power. Isaiah's salvation-oracle formula of fearlessness-through-divine-strength stands behind the verse.

echoes.text: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The 'spirit of power' contrasted with fear echoes 'not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit'; the divine Spirit as the true source of effective strength. Faint conceptual link, marked contested.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'Don't be ashamed of the testimony' draws on the Servant's resolve: 'I have set my face like a flint, and I know I will not be put to shame.' The vindication-of-the-unashamed-witness motif shapes Paul's appeal to Timothy to embrace suffering without shame.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of your testimonies before kings, and will not be put to shame' directly anticipates Paul's call not to be ashamed of the testimony and of his chains. The unashamed public confession before rulers is the psalmist's posture.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: God 'saved us and called us... not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace' restates the Deuteronomic logic of election: the LORD set his love on Israel not because of their numbers or merit but because he loved them and kept his oath. Election by sheer gracious purpose is the OT root.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: Christ 'who abolished death' echoes the eschatological promise that the LORD 'will swallow up death forever.' The abolition-of-death motif is the climactic Isaianic hope now realized in the Savior's appearing.

echoes.text: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being;
echoes.note: Christ 'brought life and immortality to light' resonates with Wisdom's claim that God created humanity for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity. The deuterocanonical immortality/incorruption vocabulary directly underlies Paul's athanasia language.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality;
echoes.note: The hope that 'the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God' and their 'hope is full of immortality' parallels the life-and-immortality brought to light through the gospel. Wisdom's immortality theology is the closest Second-Temple antecedent.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: 'He who believes will not be put to shame' is a recurrent Pauline shame-text; here it faintly informs the unashamed-testimony theme even without citation. Marked contested.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: 'I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death' provides an OT oracle of death's defeat behind Christ's abolishing of death. Faint, overlapping with Isaiah 25:8.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The disclosure of 'life and immortality' resonates with Daniel's resurrection hope of awaking to everlasting life. The apocalyptic immortality promise is a faint backdrop to the gospel's bringing of imperishable life to light.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: Paul's appointment as 'a teacher of the Gentiles' enacts the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations,' that salvation might reach the ends of the earth. His Gentile herald-role fulfills Isaiah's light-to-the-nations mandate.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'Yet I am not ashamed' in the midst of suffering reprises the Servant's flint-faced confidence that he will not be put to shame. The Servant's unashamed endurance models Paul's own.

echoes.text: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.
echoes.note: 'I know whom I have believed, and... he is able to guard that which I have committed to him' echoes 'Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me.' The committing/entrusting of oneself to the faithful God parallels the psalmist's deposit. Marked contested.

echoes.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you. In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
echoes.note: 'In God I trust; I will not be afraid' parallels Paul's confident 'I know whom I have believed' and lack of shame. Faint trust-formula resonance.

echoes.text: Therefore you shall lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul. You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them your children, talking of them, when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
echoes.note: 'Guard' the good deposit through the Spirit echoes the command to lay up God's words in heart and soul, binding and teaching them. The entrusted-treasure-of-the-word imagery is rooted in Deuteronomy's commands to keep and transmit the torah.

echoes.text: Take firm hold of instruction. Don’t let her go. Keep her, for she is your life.
echoes.note: 'Take hold of instruction; do not let go; keep her, for she is your life' closely parallels 'hold the pattern of sound words' and 'guard' the deposit. The wisdom command to grip and guard saving instruction undergirds Paul's exhortation.

echoes.text: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.
echoes.note: Holding 'the pattern of sound words' and guarding 'that good thing committed to you' draws on the Deuteronomic charge to add nothing and take nothing from the commanded word but to keep it. The deposit-of-teaching motif reflects covenant-word preservation.

echoes.text: My son, if you will receive my words, and store up my commandments within you;
echoes.note: Receiving words and 'treasuring up' commandments parallels the entrusted good deposit to be guarded. Faint wisdom-deposit link, marked contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: Zechariah's word that the great 'mountain' shall become a plain before Zerubbabel by the Spirit, not by might, is the canonical pairing of faith with the moving/leveling of an immovable obstacle. The mountain-removed-by-faith logic gives Coherence with 'faith like a mustard seed,' though Luke uses a sycamore-into-sea rather than a mountain, lowering Volume.

echoes.text: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;
echoes.note: The psalm's confidence even 'though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of an immovable thing thrown into the sea, here recast as the work of faith. The verbal overlap (uprooted/carried into the sea) is real but the figure is proverbial, so it is faint.

echoes.text: He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains were crumbled. The age-old hills collapsed. His ways are eternal.
echoes.note: The theophany that scatters the everlasting mountains coheres with the faith-moves-mountains topos behind the uprooted-tree saying. The connection is conceptual and diffuse, so confidence is low.

echoes.text: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you, neither shall my covenant of peace be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'the mountains may depart' as a figure of cosmic upheaval feeds the same stock of immovable-object-displaced imagery that the mustard-seed/sycamore saying exploits. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him, that you make your ways perfect?
echoes.note: Eliphaz asks whether a man can be profitable to God or whether it is gain to the Almighty that one is righteous, the wisdom premise that human service places God under no obligation. This grounds the 'we are unworthy servants, we have only done our duty' logic; moderate Coherence with the servant parable.

echoes.text: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?
echoes.note: Elihu's 'if you are righteous, what do you give him?' states the same theology of non-meritorious obedience underlying the unprofitable-servant saying. Recurrence of the motif across Job strengthens the Availability and Coherence, though there is no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.
echoes.note: The image of servants' eyes fixed on the hand of their master, waiting on his command, supplies the master-servant deference picture the parable assumes. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: God's claim that the Israelites are his servants whom he brought out of Egypt frames Israel's whole obedience as owed service, the covenantal backdrop to 'we have only done what was our duty.' Faint, diffuse, contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: How long, O Lord, must we cry for help?
Increase our faith, O Lord.
The righteous shall live by their faith.
Increase our faith, O Lord.
Be still before the Lord, and wait patiently.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: The prophet stands at the watchpost and shouts into the silence: how long, how long?
Increase our faith, O Lord.
And the answer comes slowly: the vision waits for its time; the righteous live by faith.
Increase our faith, O Lord.
Even faith the size of a mustard seed is enough for the God who keeps his word.
Increase our faith, O Lord.
So we wait, not idle but trusting, doing the work given us, leaving the rest to God.
Increase our faith, O Lord!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: How long, O Lord? The watchman cries into the silence.
Increase our faith, O Lord.
The righteous live by faith; the vision keeps its time.
Increase our faith, O Lord.
Faith like a mustard seed is enough.
Increase our faith, O Lord. Amen.
